reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / WHO Classification of Endocrine Tumours
clinicalPearls: A rare cause of primary hyperparathyroidism that classically produces markedly higher serum calcium and PTH than a benign adenoma, often with severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia
A palpable neck mass in a patient with primary hyperparathyroidism is an important clue, as benign adenomas are almost never palpable
End-organ damage is frequently prominent, with renal stones or impairment and overt bone disease at presentation
Many tumours harbour inactivation of the CDC73 (HRPT2) tumour-suppressor gene, and germline mutations underlie the hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome
Histological diagnosis can be difficult, relying on capsular or vascular invasion or metastasis, and definitive malignancy may only be evident with local recurrence or spread
The best chance of cure is a complete en-bloc resection at the first operation, avoiding capsular rupture and tumour spillage
Control of life-threatening hypercalcaemia with fluids and calcium-lowering measures, and use of calcimimetics for persistent disease, are central to management
reference.pathophysiology: Parathyroid carcinoma is a rare malignancy of the parathyroid chief cells that secretes excessive parathyroid hormone, driving severe hypercalcaemia through increased bone resorption, renal calcium reabsorption, and vitamin D-mediated intestinal calcium absorption. A substantial proportion of tumours show inactivation of the CDC73 (HRPT2) tumour-suppressor gene, with germline mutations causing the hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome and predisposing to malignancy. Distinguishing carcinoma from atypical adenoma is challenging histologically and rests on unequivocal invasion of the capsule or vessels, invasion of adjacent structures, or metastasis, so the diagnosis is sometimes confirmed only when the disease recurs or spreads.
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium and intact PTH, characteristically both markedly elevated
Renal function and imaging for nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis
Assessment of bone disease including bone density and skeletal imaging
Neck ultrasound and sestamibi or 4D-CT localisation, noting features suggesting invasion
CDC73 (HRPT2) germline testing and evaluation for hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome
Cross-sectional imaging to detect nodal or distant metastasis in aggressive disease
redFlags: Severe symptomatic hypercalcaemia or hypercalcaemic crisis with dehydration, confusion, and cardiac effects
A palpable neck mass accompanying primary hyperparathyroidism
Very high PTH and calcium far exceeding the usual adenoma range
Local recurrence, hoarseness, or distant metastasis indicating malignant behaviour
reference.prognosis: Complete initial en-bloc resection offers the best outcome, but the tumour tends to recur locally and metastasise late; morbidity and mortality are driven largely by uncontrolled hypercalcaemia rather than tumour bulk.
pitfalls: Mistaking carcinoma for a benign adenoma intraoperatively and rupturing the capsule, causing tumour seeding
Attributing very high calcium and PTH with a palpable mass to a simple adenoma
Relying on histology alone for diagnosis when features overlap with atypical adenoma
Overlooking a germline CDC73 mutation and the associated familial syndrome
references: WHO Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
management: Achieve cure through complete en-bloc surgical resection at the first operation, removing the tumour with its capsule intact and avoiding rupture or spillage
Control severe hypercalcaemia perioperatively and in recurrence with saline rehydration, an intravenous bisphosphonate or denosumab, and the calcimimetic cinacalcet
Reoperate for resectable local recurrence or metastasis, as debulking helps control the hormone-driven hypercalcaemia that determines morbidity
Offer CDC73 (HRPT2) germline testing and screen for the hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome, with genetic counselling and family screening
Reserve external-beam radiotherapy or systemic therapy for unresectable or progressive disease as adjuncts
Monitor serum calcium and intact PTH long-term as the key markers of recurrence, with cross-sectional imaging for nodal and distant spread
Manage within an endocrine surgery and endocrinology multidisciplinary team
